title: UNIT 1: ACID–BASE EQUILIBRIA
notes: ✓ Acid–base equilibria → Deals with the behavior of acids and bases in aqueous solutions, their strengths, ionization, buffers, salt hydrolysis, indicators, and acid–base titrations.

title: 1.1 ACID–BASE CONCEPTS
notes:
◆ THREE MAJOR THEORIES

✓ Arrhenius concept
✓ Brønsted–Lowry concept
✓ Lewis concept

✓ Each theory → Gives a broader explanation of acid–base behavior.

title: 1.1.1 ARRHENIUS CONCEPT
notes:
✓ Arrhenius acid → A substance that produces H⁺ ions when dissolved in water.

✓ Arrhenius base → A substance that produces OH⁻ ions when dissolved in water.

◆ EXAMPLE OF AN ARRHENIUS ACID
HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻

◆ EXAMPLE OF AN ARRHENIUS BASE
NaOH → Na⁺ + OH⁻

◆ NEUTRALIZATION
H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O

◆ EXAMPLE
HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O

◆ EXAM TIP
✓ Arrhenius concept → Mainly applies to acid–base behavior in aqueous solutions.

title: 1.1.2 BRØNSTED–LOWRY CONCEPT
notes:
✓ Brønsted–Lowry acid → A proton (H⁺) donor.
✓ Brønsted–Lowry base → A proton (H⁺) acceptor.

◆ EXAMPLE
HCl + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻

✓ HCl → Donates H⁺, so HCl is the acid.
✓ H₂O → Accepts H⁺, so H₂O is the base.

✓ Conjugate base → The substance formed after an acid loses H⁺.
✓ Conjugate acid → The substance formed after a base gains H⁺.

◆ REMEMBER
✓ Conjugate acid–base pair → Two species that differ by one H⁺ ion.

title: CONJUGATE ACID–BASE PAIRS
notes:
✓ Conjugate acid–base pair → Consists of two species that differ by one proton (H⁺).

◆ EXAMPLE
NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻

✓ NH₃ → Base.
✓ NH₄⁺ → Conjugate acid.
✓ H₂O → Acid.
✓ OH⁻ → Conjugate base.

◆ QUICK TIP
✓ Loses H⁺ → Becomes its conjugate base.
✓ Gains H⁺ → Becomes its conjugate acid.

title: 1.1.3 LEWIS CONCEPT
notes:
✓ Lewis acid → An electron-pair acceptor.
✓ Lewis base → An electron-pair donor.

◆ EXAMPLE
BF₃ + NH₃ → BF₃NH₃

✓ BF₃ → Accepts an electron pair, so it is the Lewis acid.
✓ NH₃ → Donates an electron pair, so it is the Lewis base.

◆ MEMORY TIP
✓ Lewis acid → Accepts an electron pair.
✓ Lewis base → Donates an electron pair.

title: THREE ACID–BASE THEORIES
notes:
◆ ARRHENIUS
✓ Acid → Produces H⁺ in water.
✓ Base → Produces OH⁻ in water.

◆ BRØNSTED–LOWRY
✓ Acid → H⁺ donor.
✓ Base → H⁺ acceptor.

◆ LEWIS
✓ Acid → Electron-pair acceptor.
✓ Base → Electron-pair donor.

◆ EASY MEMORY
✓ Arrhenius → Ions in water.
✓ Brønsted–Lowry → Proton transfer.
✓ Lewis → Electron-pair transfer.

title: 1.2 IONIC EQUILIBRIA OF WEAK ACIDS AND BASES
notes:
✓ Strong acids and bases → Ionize almost completely in water.
✓ Weak acids and bases → Ionize only partially.

✓ Weak electrolytes → Establish an equilibrium between their ionized and un-ionized forms.

◆ EXAMPLE
CH₃COOH + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + CH₃COO⁻

✓ Double arrow ⇌ → Indicates that the reaction is reversible and an equilibrium is established.

title: 1.2.1 IONIZATION OF WATER
notes:
✓ Water → Undergoes a small amount of self-ionization.

H₂O + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻

✓ Ionic product of water (Kᵥ) → The equilibrium constant for this process.

Kᵥ = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻]

◆ AT 25°C
Kᵥ = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴

✓ Pure water → [H⁺] = [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ M.
✓ Therefore → pH = 7 and pOH = 7.

◆ EXAM TIP
✓ Neutral solution at 25°C → Has equal concentrations of H⁺ and OH⁻.

title: pH AND pOH
notes:
✓ pH → Used to express the acidity of a solution.
pH = −log[H⁺]

✓ pOH → Used to express the basicity of a solution.
pOH = −log[OH⁻]

◆ AT 25°C
✓ pH + pOH = 14

◆ GENERAL RULE
✓ pH < 7 → Acidic.
✓ pH = 7 → Neutral.
✓ pH > 7 → Basic.

◆ EXAMPLE
If [H⁺] = 1 × 10⁻³ M:
pH = −log(1 × 10⁻³)
pH = 3

✓ Therefore → The solution is acidic.

title: 1.2.2 STRENGTH OF ACIDS AND BASES
notes:
✓ Acid strength → Depends on how easily an acid donates H⁺ ions.

✓ Strong acids → Ionize almost completely in water.
✓ Examples → HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, HClO₄, and H₂SO₄.

✓ Weak acids → Ionize only partially.
✓ Examples → CH₃COOH, HF, and H₂CO₃.

✓ Strong bases → Ionize almost completely.
✓ Weak bases → Ionize only partially.

◆ IMPORTANT
✓ Acid strength ≠ acid concentration.
✓ Strong acid → Can be dilute.
✓ Weak acid → Can be concentrated.

title: ACID DISSOCIATION CONSTANT — Kₐ
notes:
◆ FOR A WEAK ACID
HA + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + A⁻

Kₐ = [H₃O⁺][A⁻] / [HA]

✓ Larger Kₐ → Greater ionization and stronger acid.
✓ Smaller Kₐ → Less ionization and weaker acid.

◆ EXAM TIP
✓ Comparing weak acids → The acid with the larger Kₐ is generally the stronger acid.

title: BASE DISSOCIATION CONSTANT — Kᵦ
notes:
◆ FOR A WEAK BASE
B + H₂O ⇌ BH⁺ + OH⁻

Kᵦ = [BH⁺][OH⁻] / [B]

✓ Larger Kᵦ → Greater ionization and stronger base.
✓ Smaller Kᵦ → Less ionization and weaker base.

title: RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN Kₐ AND Kᵦ
notes:
✓ For a conjugate acid–base pair → Kₐ × Kᵦ = Kᵥ.

✓ At 25°C → Kₐ × Kᵦ = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴.

✓ Logarithmic relationship → pKₐ + pKᵦ = 14.

◆ REMEMBER
✓ Strong acid → Weak conjugate base.
✓ Strong base → Weak conjugate acid.

title: 1.3 COMMON-ION EFFECT
notes:
✓ Common-ion effect → Suppression of the ionization of a weak electrolyte when another electrolyte containing a common ion is added.

◆ EXAMPLE
CH₃COOH ⇌ H⁺ + CH₃COO⁻

CH₃COONa → Na⁺ + CH₃COO⁻

✓ Adding CH₃COONa → Increases the concentration of CH₃COO⁻.
✓ According to Le Chatelier's principle → The equilibrium shifts to the left.
✓ Therefore → The ionization of CH₃COOH decreases.

◆ EXAM TIP
✓ Adding a common ion → Generally decreases the ionization of a weak electrolyte.

title: 1.3.2 BUFFER SOLUTIONS
notes:
✓ Buffer solution → A solution that resists significant changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added.

◆ ACIDIC BUFFER
✓ Made from → A weak acid and its conjugate base or salt.
✓ Example → CH₃COOH + CH₃COONa.

◆ BASIC BUFFER
✓ Made from → A weak base and its conjugate acid or salt.
✓ Example → NH₃ + NH₄Cl.

✓ Buffers → Help maintain a nearly constant pH.

title: HENDERSON–HASSELBALCH EQUATION
notes:
◆ FOR AN ACIDIC BUFFER
pH = pKₐ + log([A⁻] / [HA])

◆ WHERE
✓ HA → Weak acid.
✓ A⁻ → Conjugate base.

◆ SPECIAL CASE
✓ If [A⁻] = [HA] → pH = pKₐ.

◆ EXAM TIP
✓ Equal concentrations of weak acid and conjugate base → Buffer pH equals pKₐ.

title: 1.4 HYDROLYSIS OF SALTS
notes:
✓ Salt hydrolysis → Reaction of ions from a salt with water to produce an acidic or basic solution.

✓ pH of a salt solution → Depends on the strengths of the acid and base from which the salt was formed.

title: 1.4.1 STRONG ACID + STRONG BASE
notes:
✓ Salt formed from a strong acid and a strong base → Generally does not undergo significant hydrolysis.

◆ EXAMPLE
HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O

✓ NaCl solution → Approximately neutral.
✓ At 25°C → pH ≈ 7.

◆ REMEMBER
✓ Strong acid + strong base → Approximately neutral salt solution.

title: 1.4.2 WEAK ACID + STRONG BASE
notes:
✓ Salt formed from a weak acid and a strong base → Produces a basic solution.

◆ EXAMPLE
CH₃COONa

CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻

✓ OH⁻ is produced → The solution becomes basic.

◆ REMEMBER
✓ Weak acid + strong base → Basic salt solution.

title: 1.4.3 STRONG ACID + WEAK BASE
notes:
✓ Salt formed from a strong acid and a weak base → Produces an acidic solution.

◆ EXAMPLE
NH₄Cl

NH₄⁺ + H₂O ⇌ NH₃ + H₃O⁺

✓ H₃O⁺ is produced → The solution becomes acidic.

◆ REMEMBER
✓ Strong acid + weak base → Acidic salt solution.

title: 1.4.4 WEAK ACID + WEAK BASE
notes:
✓ Salt formed from a weak acid and a weak base → Both ions may undergo hydrolysis.

✓ Final pH → Depends on the relative values of Kₐ and Kᵦ.

✓ Kₐ > Kᵦ → Solution tends to be acidic.
✓ Kᵦ > Kₐ → Solution tends to be basic.
✓ Kₐ ≈ Kᵦ → Solution may be approximately neutral.

title: SALT HYDROLYSIS QUICK TABLE
notes:
✓ Strong acid + strong base → Neutral.
✓ Weak acid + strong base → Basic.
✓ Strong acid + weak base → Acidic.
✓ Weak acid + weak base → Depends on Kₐ and Kᵦ.

◆ EXAM FOCUS
✓ Salt hydrolysis → Very important for determining the pH of salt solutions.

title: 1.5 ACID–BASE INDICATORS
notes:
✓ Acid–base indicator → A substance that changes color over a particular pH range.
✓ Indicators → Are usually weak acids or weak bases.

✓ General representation → HIn ⇌ H⁺ + In⁻
✓ HIn and In⁻ → Have different colors.

title: COMMON ACID–BASE INDICATORS
notes:
◆ LITMUS
✓ Acidic → Red.
✓ Basic → Blue.

◆ METHYL ORANGE
✓ Acidic → Red.
✓ Basic → Yellow.

◆ PHENOLPHTHALEIN
✓ Acidic → Colorless.
✓ Basic → Pink.

◆ IMPORTANT
✓ Indicator → Changes color over a pH transition range rather than at one exact pH.

title: 1.5.2 EQUIVALENTS OF ACIDS AND BASES
notes:
✓ Equivalent → Represents the amount of a substance that supplies or reacts with one mole of H⁺ or OH⁻, depending on the reaction.

✓ Number of equivalents = moles × n-factor.

✓ n-factor → Depends on the number of H⁺ ions donated or OH⁻ ions supplied in the reaction.

◆ EXAMPLES
✓ HCl → n-factor = 1.
✓ H₂SO₄ → n-factor = 2 when both acidic protons react.

title: 1.5.3 ACID–BASE TITRATIONS
notes:
✓ Acid–base titration → Laboratory method used to determine the concentration of an acid or base by reacting it with a solution of known concentration.

◆ TITRANT
✓ Titrant → Solution with known concentration.

◆ ANALYTE
✓ Analyte → Solution whose concentration is being determined.

◆ EQUIVALENCE POINT
✓ Equivalence point → Point at which the reacting substances are present in their stoichiometrically equivalent amounts.

◆ ENDPOINT
✓ Endpoint → Point at which the indicator changes color.

◆ GENERAL NEUTRALIZATION
✓ Acid + Base → Salt + Water.

title: TITRATION FORMULA
notes:
◆ FOR A SIMPLE 1:1 ACID–BASE REACTION
M₁V₁ = M₂V₂

✓ This equation → Should only be used directly when the stoichiometric ratio is 1:1.

✓ Different coefficients → Require the balanced chemical equation and stoichiometric ratios.

◆ EXAM TIP
✓ Always balance the chemical equation → Before solving a titration problem.

title: UNIT 1 — MUST REMEMBER
notes:
◆ ARRHENIUS
✓ Acid → Produces H⁺.
✓ Base → Produces OH⁻.

◆ BRØNSTED–LOWRY
✓ Acid → H⁺ donor.
✓ Base → H⁺ acceptor.

◆ LEWIS
✓ Acid → Electron-pair acceptor.
✓ Base → Electron-pair donor.

◆ IMPORTANT FORMULAS
✓ Kᵥ = [H⁺][OH⁻]
✓ pH = −log[H⁺]
✓ pOH = −log[OH⁻]
✓ pH + pOH = 14 at 25°C.
✓ Kₐ = [H⁺][A⁻] / [HA]
✓ Kᵦ = [BH⁺][OH⁻] / [B]
✓ Kₐ × Kᵦ = Kᵥ
✓ pKₐ + pKᵦ = 14 at 25°C.
✓ pH = pKₐ + log([A⁻]/[HA]).

title: COMMON EXAM TRAPS
notes:
◆ 1. STRONG ≠ CONCENTRATED
✓ Strong acid → Ionizes almost completely.
✓ Concentration → Tells how much solute is present per unit volume.

◆ 2. ACID STRENGTH ≠ pH
✓ pH → Also depends on concentration.

◆ 3. BRØNSTED–LOWRY ≠ LEWIS
✓ Brønsted–Lowry → Focuses on proton transfer.
✓ Lewis → Focuses on electron-pair transfer.

◆ 4. Kₐ ≠ Kᵦ
✓ Kₐ → Describes acid strength.
✓ Kᵦ → Describes base strength.

◆ 5. EQUIVALENCE POINT ≠ ENDPOINT
✓ Equivalence point → Based on stoichiometry.
✓ Endpoint → Observed through the indicator color change.
